doc.title: Bernard Purdie interviewed by Monk Rowe, West Orange, New Jersey, July 30, 2003

title: Leader and follower; locking in with Bucky Pizzarelli
summary: Purdie describes being a natural leader and follower, early demo work, and how he locked in with guitarist Bucky Pizzarelli and the bass player.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: wrong. And the part that hurts the most is that I was always right. They did not like it and I can’t blame them. I mean it took me years to understand that, but the point was was that I just had this instinct. And I had it all my life, to make things work. Just make it work. Always thinking about making it work. Putting things together. I could always put things together. I could always put people together. I could always put places together. I could always. I mean I was a natural leader. But I was a great follower. And that’s what you have to be. That’s what I was taught. In order to be a good leader, you must be a great follower. Because unless you let the people know where you’re going or where they’re going, they’re not going to follow you, for you to be a leader. You have to learn something about being a follower. So I had great teachers, and they showed me all those things as I was coming along. So I knew that I was a great follower. I didn’t know I was a great leader. That took a long time for me to know and to understand that. And then of course my ego got in the way in the early parts of my life in the twenties. Because all of a sudden I’m doing all of this work and recording, and people are coming to me and wanting me to be on the date. And I always spoke up. I’ve never not spoken. Oh no. And one of the people that we talked about earlier, Bucky Pizzarelli, he was one of the first ones. He would sit over there and look at me and he’d say “go on, Purdie, go on, Purdie.” And we’d just groove. We instantly hit it off, the first time that we were doing demos.
Rock & roll type demos? R&B things?

Yes, yes. We were doing that. And he was with that guitar and his body, you know his head, shoulders was happening. It wasn’t all about his body and, but the foot was going. But it was just here. Woo. And that hand. I didn’t have to look at his hand, I could see it. I could feel it. I could close my eyes and see him playing on the parts. Because I knew music. I didn’t have any problem there. But woo, man, hit me deep, go right to the soul no matter what he played. And rhythm was the first thing that he would play, no matter what kind of melody that anybody wanted, he played rhythm first and then sneaked the melody in. But it was something else. I mean that to me is how you put folks together. You lock folks in. Guitar, bass, piano. The drummer — if he’s got the bass player, which is of course for the drummer is number one, the bass player is number one — then he has to make a choice between guitar and piano as number two. You don’t know which one is going to be number two until you play.

Yeah. And the thing is is that Bucky’s on the date, Bucky becomes number two ninety- nine percent of the time. I don’t care who’s on the piano. When Hank Jones was on the piano I mean there’s nobody can be any finer than him playing the piano and playing chords or playing rhythm or playing melody.
